transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-01-16
- Time: 15:00 PST
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Jin (Redwood SE), Dr. Anika Rao, Tom Williams, Priya Shah, Samir Desai

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
Redwood and Lyra scoped a private-network POC. Main asks: ensure model inference stays inside Lyra's VPC/approved regions; evaluate peering vs PrivateLink; define success metrics around latency/cost/throughput; run benchmarks (chat with 2k/8k contexts, embeddings batch, bulk gen) and deliver results. Security to review SOC2 docs and KMS flow; next steps include benchmarks by SE, security packet, and pilot kickoff.

Topics:
1) Success criteria
2) Workload sizing & benchmark types
3) Network topology options (VPC Peering vs PrivateLink/Endpoint Service)
4) Regions & egress constraints
5) Data handling, KMS, audit logs
6) Timeline and next steps

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Maya (AE): okay hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm Maya from Redwood, i'll kick us off. How're we all doing?
[00:06] Anika: good, thanks. We wanted to use this call to nail down the pilot scope and make sure we don't hit any surprises around residency and egress.
[00:14] Tom: yes our infra team needs clear topology — whether it's peering or private link, and where the control plane talks out to.
[00:22] Maya: totally. Carlos and Jin from our SE team are here to go over benchmarks and runtimes. Carlos, want to take it?
[00:27] Carlos (SE): yeah thanks. Quick caveat first — transcriptions are sometimes flaky so if names get weird, sorry. We'll outline the benchmark plan. From what we heard: Lyra wants inference to live in your AWS accounts, prefer region A and region B only, no cross-region egress. Correct?
[00:42] Priya: correct. We can do us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Anything else needs an exception. Also we have strict egress policies — packets leaving our VPC to public endpoints are blocked unless whitelisted.
[00:54] Carlos: got it. Two delivery options for the POC: 1) Redwood Private with a customer VPC peering (we bring instances into your account or we peer into a dedicated account), or 2) Private Endpoint (AWS NLB + PrivateLink) where the control plane sits in Redwood but traffic to inference endpoints is via endpoint service — both keep data off the public internet.
[01:12] Samir: can you explain difference practically; our security team hates peering because it grants route-level access.
[01:18] Jin (SE): yeah, peering exposes IP routes — you need to manage route tables carefully. PrivateLink is more restrictive: it's an endpoint service, only specific ENIs get access, and you don't share routing. Many regulated customers prefer PrivateLink. But PrivateLink adds per-GB costs and some ops complexity.
[01:34] Anika: latency concern — PrivateLink adds a small hop. We care about 95th percentile latency under 200ms for chat calls with 2k context. Is that achievable?
[01:43] Carlos: that's reasonable. We'll benchmark 2k and 8k contexts. For 2k chat we expect p95 ~ 80-140ms on a dedicated gpus pool depending on model. For 8k it'll be higher, ~200-400ms p95; depends on batching. Those numbers are estimates; we'll run the actual tests.
[01:58] Tom: what models are you testing? Our workload is a fine-tuned 7B LLM and embeddings for search; about 120 requests/sec for embeddings batch jobs and ~30 rps for chat peak.
[02:10] Carlos: perfect, we'll run with a 7B LLM baseline (your fine-tuned weights if you can provide or we use an equivalent open-checkpoint) and embeddings vector size 1536. We'll size the pilot nodes to match your peak: 30 rps interactive, 120 rps batch (embeds) with expected latency SLO.
[02:24] Priya: data residency detail — inference logs and KV cache must not be stored outside the approved regions. We also need KMS integration: customer-managed keys for any persisted model artifacts and logs.
[02:34] Jin: Redwood Private supports bringing your KMS (we can handle KMS keys in your account) and we can configure audit logs to forward to your CloudWatch or S3 in-region. That will be in the security pack.
[02:45] Maya: to set success criteria would you agree to three items: 1) Functional correctness (match baseline eval metrics on sample devset), 2) Latency SLO — p95 under 200ms for 2k chats and p95 under 500ms for 8k chats, 3) Residency — all inference traffic and logs remain in approved regions with no internet egress.
[03:04] Anika: yes those seem right; also add cost threshold — we want cost per 1k tokens to be below a target, we'll give a number later.
[03:12] Maya: good. We'll add cost as a soft criteria for the pilot.
[03:15] Tom: around networking, what's the operational difference for us in setup time? Peering vs PrivateLink?
[03:20] Carlos: peering is typically faster to stand up if you control both accounts or have a shared infra team; PrivateLink requires creating endpoint services, NLBs, and cross-account endpoint configuration — takes longer but less blast radius. For the pilot estimate: peering ~ 1-2 days, PrivateLink ~ 3-7 days depending on approvals.
[03:36] Priya: approvals might push PrivateLink longer. Also we need to do an architecture review with our network team.
[03:41] Maya: understood. We'll provide a network diagram for both approaches and a checklist for required IAM roles and route table edits.
[03:48] Jin: on benchmarks — we'll run three workloads: 1) interactive chat (2k + 8k contexts), 2) embedding throughput batch (512 batch size typical), 3) bulk generation jobs (multi-token generation for fine-tuning evaluation). For each we'll record p50, p95, tail, and cost per token. We'll also run warm KV cache vs cold start to show cache benefits.
[04:09] Tom: warm vs cold is critical; our workload has cache reuse for session-based chat so warm numbers are more representative.
[04:15] Carlos: we'll include both, and show how prefix caching reduces cost and latency for your session patterns.
[04:20] Anika: about providing our models — we have a fine-tuned 7B in an S3 bucket. How do you prefer to get it?
[04:26] Jin: secure transfer via presigned S3 or we can accept AMI or container image. For Private deployments we can pull from your S3 in-account or you can push the model into a bucket we provide in your account. We'll provide exact manifests in the onboarding doc.
[04:38] Priya: encryption at rest is required for those artifacts. KMS CMK must be in our account.
[04:42] Carlos: yes; customer-managed CMK in your account is supported. We'll document the permissions needed for Redwood's service role.
[04:48] Samir: what's the control plane visibility? We want to ensure metadata doesn't leak.
[04:51] Maya: the control plane is minimal — orchestration signals and metrics can be sent to Redwood unless you opt for Private where we deploy a remote control plane into your VPC. For strict residency we can run control plane components in your account so telemetry remains in-region. That's part of the Private/on-prem offering.
[05:08] Priya: ok interesting. We need an architecture diagram showing the control plane options.
[05:12] Maya: will do.
[05:14] Jin: one more note on egress: if you choose PrivateLink we still need to pull some small external resources for model compilation or kernel fetch — we can vendor those assets into an allowlist or cache them in VPC. For full air-gapped we have an on-prem package.
[05:31] Tom: how about IAM roles — do we create cross-account roles for Redwood?
[05:35] Carlos: typically yes. For peering we need a role that grants Redwood service account permission to create ENIs and attach volumes in a dedicated sub-account or in your account depending on approach. We'll supply the least-privilege policy.
[05:46] Anika: timeline — we want a 3-week pilot. Is that realistic?
[05:50] Maya: yes, a focused 3-week pilot is doable if we get the model and network sign-offs quickly. Week 0: network + security setup, Week 1: deploy and baseline, Week 2: run benchmarks and iterate, Week 3: evaluate results and handoff.
[06:05] Priya: but getting PrivateLink approvals might push week 0 out. If network approvals are slow we may start with peering for speed and then switch to PrivateLink for production.
[06:15] Carlos: that's a common path. We'll design the pilot so artifacts are portable between topologies.
[06:20] Anika: success metrics again — when do you hand over the final report?
[06:23] Maya: we aim to deliver a written pilot report within 3 business days after the pilot ends, with raw logs, benchmark spreadsheet, and recommended config.
[06:31] Tom: what about cost reporting? We need cost per-1k tokens and projected monthly cost at scale.
[06:36] Jin: we'll include runbook with cost breakdown by model, GPU-hour estimate, and cache/batching tradeoffs.
[06:42] Priya: one more compliance ask: we need audit logs for admin actions for at least 12 months. Can you retain that?
[06:49] Carlos: yes, logs can be forwarded to your S3/CloudWatch with lifecycle policy; retention is configurable. We'll include that in the security pack.
[06:58] Anika: will you run the benchmarks from within our VPC? We prefer testing under the same network constraints.
[07:03] Carlos: yes for the Private pilot we deploy the inference nodes in your account so benchmarks are run in your network fabric; that gives most realistic numbers.
[07:11] Samir: for the pilot we can accept temporary elevated perms for the role.
[07:15] Priya: but only if we review the policy first.
[07:18] Maya: fair. We'll send the policy and the network diagram by EOD Tuesday.
[07:23] Tom: about data access — do you keep any request logs outside the region for analytics?
[07:28] Jin: we can config analytics to stream to your in-region storage; the default hosted analytics live in Redwood but for Private they'll be pushed to your account.
[07:36] Anika: ok good.
[07:38] Carlos: last technical note: we'll measure tail-latency under synthetic spike — e.g., 3x typical load for 2 minutes — to see graceful degradation and fallback to smaller model variants. That helps your SLO planning.
[07:50] Anika: fallback model variants, yes we want automatic fallback if capacity is constrained. Does Redwood support that?
[07:56] Maya: yep, routing policies can fall back to cheaper or lower-latency model variants automatically. We'll show a canary rollout as well.
[08:02] Tom: what's the data flow diagram look like for PrivateLink?
[08:06] Jin: (short verbal description) client traffic from your app -> VPC endpoint -> NLB -> Redwood endpoint service -> inference instance. Control plane calls may still be to Redwood control, but telemetry can be forwarded.
[08:18] Priya: we need to ensure there are no public NAT gateways used by inference nodes.
[08:22] Carlos: we can run node subnets private-only and ensure no NAT egress. Any third-party pulls can be pre-cached.
[08:29] Anika: ok. Another question: bench metrics — what sample size will you use for p95?
[08:33] Carlos: we typically run 10k requests for embeddings, 5k interactive sessions for chat, and multiple runs across cold/warm to get stable p95. We'll share the bench harness and test scripts so you can reproduce.
[08:45] Tom: will you open-source the harness?
[08:48] Jin: we'll share a sanitized harness and a runbook; some low-level telemetry is Redwood internal but reproducible configs are provided.
[08:55] Priya: security packet — can you list what you will include?
[08:59] Maya: SOC2 attestation, network diagrams for peering and PrivateLink, least-privilege IAM policy, KMS integration notes, audit log config, data retention & deletion process, and list of third-party dependencies.
[09:11] Priya: okay that works.
[09:13] Anika: final item — success signoff needs stakeholders: Anika for quality, Priya for security, Samir for infra. We'll sign off together.
[09:21] Maya: perfect. I'll put that in the success criteria doc.
[09:24] -- Wrap up / Recap --
[09:25] Maya: recap: Redwood to provide security pack by 2027-01-19, SE to share initial benchmark plan and run first bench by 2027-01-23, pricing and pilot commitment options by 2027-01-18, and kickoff scheduled 2027-01-25 pending network approvals. Pilot target weeks: 3-week run.
[09:42] Tom: sounds good.
[09:44] Anika: thanks everyone.
[09:46] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in email with the attachments.
[09:50] (call ends)
